title: Recursion and Divide-and-Conquer: Solve Big Problems with Small Ones

questions.question: Every recursive definition must have which two ingredients?
options: A base case and a recursive case
questions.rationale: The base case is answered directly with no self-call; the recursive case restates the problem in terms of smaller input.

questions.question: What happens when a recursive function's base case is missing or unreachable?
options: It loops forever without using memory
Each call pushes a frame until a stack overflow kills the program
The compiler converts it to iteration
questions.rationale: Without a base case the calls never bottom out; every call pushes a stack frame until the program dies with a stack overflow.

questions.question: What is the approximate cost of the naive recursive Fibonacci algorithm?
questions.rationale: The naive call tree recomputes overlapping subproblems — fib(3) twice, fib(2) three times — and the branching roughly doubles each level, giving about O(2ⁿ).

questions.question: With memoization, Fibonacci's cost becomes:
options: O(n) time at the price of O(n) memory
questions.rationale: Memoization records each answer at first computation, so repeats become lookups: Fibonacci drops from O(2ⁿ) to O(n) time for O(n) memory.

questions.question: How many moves does Tower of Hanoi require for n discs?
questions.rationale: The recurrence h(n) = 2·h(n−1) + 1 resolves to 2ⁿ − 1 moves; 64 discs take about 585 billion years at one move per second.

questions.question: Which recurrence describes Euclid's GCD algorithm?
options: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)
gcd(a, b) = gcd(a mod b, a)
questions.rationale: Euclid's GCD recurses with gcd(b, a mod b) and costs O(log min(a, b)) because the shrink is multiplicative.

questions.question: The three phases of divide-and-conquer are:
questions.rationale: Divide the problem into smaller instances, conquer each piece recursively, then combine the answers into the final result.

questions.question: About how many comparisons does binary search need among 1,000,000 sorted items?
questions.rationale: Each comparison halves the range, so log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20 comparisons — by step 20 only about 1 item remains possible.

questions.question: How does tabulation differ from memoization?
options: Tabulation is top-down recursion with a cache
Tabulation fills a table with loops, computing every state up to n
Tabulation cannot be used for Fibonacci
questions.rationale: Tabulation is the bottom-up approach — loops fill the table for every state up to n — while memoization is top-down recursion plus a cache that only computes needed states.

questions.question: What is tail recursion?
options: A recursion with two base cases
A recursion whose self-call is the last action, with nothing pending afterwards
A recursion that runs in O(log n)
A recursion stored on the heap instead of the stack
questions.rationale: Tail recursion — the self-call is the last action — can be compiled into a loop, but Python does not, so deep recursion there must become an explicit loop with a stack.
